definition: Add short notes to a diagram or graph, such as naming a peak, a bond or a stage of a reaction, right where it appears.

Work out a number and show the stages that lead to it, such as moles, then mass. Give the final value with units and sensible significant figures, because the working can still earn marks if the answer slips.
Make a short judgement about a statement or a result you have found, such as whether an experimental value is close to the literature value. Give the reason.
Say what two or more things have in common, mentioning each one in every point you make, such as "both ions have the same electron configuration".
Say how two or more things differ, mentioning each one in every point you make, such as "diamond has no free electrons, while graphite has delocalized electrons".
Draw a conclusion that follows from the information given, such as a formula from a spectrum or an order from rate data. Show the short chain of reasoning that gets you there.
Give a full account in words of what happens or what is seen, such as a colour change or a trend down a group. Reasons are not needed unless asked for.
Find the one answer that fits the information, such as an empirical formula or an enthalpy change, with the working that gets you there.
Weigh up a range of arguments or factors on more than one side, such as the benefits and drawbacks of a fuel. Back each point with evidence and end with a clear conclusion.

Make an accurate, labelled diagram or graph in pencil, using a ruler for straight lines. For a Lewis formula or mechanism, show every lone pair, charge and curly arrow, because each one can carry a mark.
Give a sensible approximate value, and show where it comes from, such as a reading from a graph or a trend in a data table.
Judge something by weighing up its strengths and its limitations, such as a method or a model. Give both sides, not just one.
Say why or how, giving reasons or causes. Link the observation to the particles, such as stronger forces between molecules leading to a higher boiling point.
Give a brief account or summary of the main points, without full detail. One clear point per mark is usually enough.
Give the result you expect, such as the direction an equilibrium shifts or the product of a reaction. A reason is only needed if the question asks for one.
Draw the right general shape, not to scale, with the relevant features labelled, such as the axes, the activation energy on an energy profile or the equivalence point on a titration curve.
Give a short answer, such as a name, value, formula or equation, with no working or explanation needed.
Put forward a sensible possible answer, such as a reason for an error or an improvement to a method, often in an unfamiliar setting. It needs to fit the chemistry, not to be the only answer.
